title: As if
intro: *Gibi* (like) after a noun came in [A2 unit 8](gp-equative): *çocuk gibi*. After a verb it compares whole situations: `-mIş gibi` means **as if** (*Hiçbir şey olmamış gibi davrandı*), and `-mIş gibi yapmak` means **to pretend**. Written Turkish has a one-word **as if**, `-cAsInA`. After participles *gibi* gives **as I said** and **it looks as if**, and *sanki* opens a comparison on its own.

sections.title: Olmamış gibi: as if it had happened

blocks.text: Put *gibi* after a verb in `-mIş` and it means **as if**: *Hiçbir şey olmamış gibi davrandı* (She acted as if nothing had happened). This is the `-mIş` of hearsay and inference ([B1 unit 3](gp-evidential-mis)), and it keeps a trace of that meaning: what follows *gibi* is only an appearance, not a fact.

**Which -mIş?** The clause keeps its own tense before `-mIş`. Plain `-mIş` for something completed: *görmemiş gibi* (as if he hadn't seen). `-(I)yormuş` for something in progress: *anlamıyormuş gibi* (as if she didn't understand). `-(y)AcAkmIş` for something about to happen: *ağlayacakmış gibi* (as if she were about to cry). Nouns, adjectives, *var* and *yok* take `-(y)mIş` ([A2 unit 2](gp-idi-imis)): *hastaymış gibi* (as if he were ill), *yokmuş gibi* (as if it weren't there).

head: As if…
Meaning
rows: as if she were about to cry
as if she owned the house

blocks.text: **Persons.** When the subject of the *gibi* clause differs from the main verb's, add its ending after `-mIş`, the type I endings of **to be**: *Bana suçluymuşum gibi baktı* (He looked at me as if I were guilty). With the same subject, the bare *-mIş* is usual: *Hiçbir şey duymamış gibi davrandım* (I acted as if I hadn't heard anything); *duymamışım gibi* is also correct.

rows.en: as if he or she hadn't heard
as if you hadn't heard (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **The main verb.** The clause usually goes with *davranmak* (to behave; to treat someone), *konuşmak*, *bakmak* and *görünmek* (to look, to seem). With *gelmek* and the dative it describes a feeling: *Bana hiç uyumamışım gibi geliyor* (I feel as if I haven't slept at all).

items.en: She acted as if nothing had happened.

items.tr: Beni hiç görmemiş gibi yanımdan geçti.
items.seg: Beni hiç gör|me|miş gibi yanımdan geçti.
items.en: He walked past me as if he'd never seen me.
He looked at me as if I were guilty.
She spoke in a voice as if she were about to cry.
He acts as if he owned the house.
They treated us as if we were strangers.

blocks.text: *Hiçbir şey olmadı gibi* is wrong: before *gibi*, the verb takes `-mIş`, never `-DI`. The `-DI` form states a fact; *gibi* needs an appearance.
*Davranmak* takes the person it concerns in the dative: *Bana çocuk gibi davranma* (Don't treat me like a child), *Misafirlere iyi davrandılar* (They treated the guests well).

*Gibi yapmak*, literally **to do as if**, means **to pretend**: *Uyuyormuş gibi yaptı* (She pretended to be asleep). The pretended state takes the `-mIş` forms of the previous section, and the person and the tense go on *yapmak*: *Anlamış gibi yaptım* (I pretended to understand), *Dinliyormuş gibi yapıyor* (He's pretending to listen).

blocks.caption: `-mIş` or `-(I)yormuş`?
head: Turkish
Meaning
rows: She pretended to understand (to have understood).
He pretended not to have seen.

rows.en: he or she pretended to be asleep
you pretended to be asleep (plural or polite)

blocks.text: The `-mIş` form stays bare with *yapmak*: *uyuyormuş gibi yaptım*, not *uyuyormuşum gibi yaptım*. Every tense of *yapmak* works: *yapıyor* (is pretending), *yapardı* (used to pretend), *yapma!* (don't pretend).
**Not pretending to.** Negate the pretended state, not *yapmak*: *Duymamış gibi yaptı* (He pretended not to have heard). *Duymuş gibi yapmadı* says he **didn't pretend** to have heard.

**Everyday alternatives.** *Numara yapmak* is colloquial for **to fake it, to put on an act**: *Numara yapma!* (Stop faking!), *hasta numarası yapmak* (to pretend to be ill). *Rol yapmak* is **to act a part, to put on an act**. *Taklit etmek* is **to imitate** someone: *Öğretmenini taklit ediyor* (He's imitating his teacher).

items.en: She pretended to be asleep.
He pretended not to have heard.
Don't pretend you don't know anything!

items.tr: Ders çalışıyormuş gibi yapıyor, ama aslında telefonla oynuyor.
items.seg: Ders çalış|ıyor|muş gibi yapıyor, ama aslında telefonla oynuyor.
items.en: He's pretending to study, but he's actually playing on his phone.
She's pretending to be ill.

blocks.text: English **pretend to** takes an infinitive; Turkish never does. *Uyumak gibi yaptı* is wrong: the pretended state goes into `-mIş` or `-(I)yormuş`, *uyuyormuş gibi yaptı*.
Like French **faire semblant de**, *gibi yapmak* is built on **do**: *faire semblant de dormir*, *uyuyormuş gibi yapmak*. But Turkish puts the state in `-mIş`, where French uses the infinitive.

Written Turkish has a one-word **as if**, `-cAsInA`, added to the same forms as *gibi*: *Hiçbir şey olmamışçasına gülümsedi* (She smiled as if nothing had happened). It belongs to novels, stories, news and speeches. In conversation, `-mIş gibi` is the usual choice, and means the same.

head: Form
Example
Meaning
rows: as if she were about to cry
almost running, as if at a run

blocks.text: **-(I)rcAsInA**, on the aorist, compares the manner of an action: *Koşarcasına yürüyordu* (He was walking almost at a run), *Yalvarırcasına baktı* (She looked at me pleadingly). Some are close to set phrases: *bilircesine* (as if he knew), *kırarcasına* (hard enough to break something).

**On nouns and adjectives** it gives adverbs of manner, several of them everyday words: *delicesine* (madly), *çılgıncasına* (wildly), *aptalcasına* (stupidly), *kahramancasına* (heroically): *Onu delicesine seviyor* (He loves her madly).

items.en: She smiled as if nothing had happened.
He was walking almost at a run.
She looked at me pleadingly.
He talks as if he knew everything.
Her heart was pounding as if it would leap out of her chest.
He loves her madly.

blocks.text: `-cAsInA` has only two vowel patterns: its I follows the A, so *olmuşçasına*, never *olmuşçusuna*. Its first letter is ç after a voiceless consonant, as with every C suffix: *olmamışçasına*, but *koşarcasına*.
Don't confuse it with `-CA` ([A2 unit 12](gp-ca)): *yavaşça* (slowly), *Türkçe*. `-cAsInA` always compares: *deli gibi*, **like a madman**, is *delicesine*.

**-DIğI gibi: as, the way.** After an object participle ([B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik)), *gibi* means **as** or **the way**: *Dediğim gibi* (As I said), *Bildiğiniz gibi* (As you know), *İstediğin gibi yap* (Do it the way you like). The participle keeps its possessive: *dediğin gibi* (as you said), *anlattığı gibi* (as she told it).

In a story, `-DIğI gibi` can also mean **as soon as**, like `-(I)r -mAz` ([B1 unit 8](gp-r-maz)): *Eve geldiği gibi yattı* (He went to bed as soon as he got home). The verbs around it make the meaning clear.

**-(y)AcAk gibi: it looks as if.** With the bare future participle, *gibi* is a forecast from what you see: *Yağmur yağacak gibi* (It looks like it's going to rain), *Bu iş bitecek gibi değil* (This job doesn't look like it'll ever be finished). *Yağacakmış gibi*, from the first section, only compares: **as if it were going to rain**.

**-(y)AcAk gibi olmak: to nearly, to feel about to.** With *olmak*, usually in the past, it describes a moment that came close: *Merdivende düşecek gibi oldum* (I nearly fell on the stairs), *Sıcaktan bayılacak gibi oldum* (I felt I was going to faint from the heat). Nothing happened in the end.

**Sanki: as if, it's as though.** *Sanki* opens a comparison, often together with `-mIş gibi`: *Sanki hiçbir şey olmamış gibi konuşuyor* (He's talking as if nothing had happened). With an ordinary tense it gives an impression: *Sanki bir rüyadayım* (It's as if I'm in a dream), *Sanki biri kapıyı çaldı* (I think someone knocked; it sounded as if someone knocked). *Tıpkı* strengthens *gibi* after a noun: *Tıpkı annesi gibi konuşuyor* (She talks just like her mother).

items.en: As I said, I'm not in the office tomorrow.
As you know, the meeting is at three.
He went to bed as soon as he got home.
It looks like it's going to rain.
I nearly fell on the stairs.
It's as if I'm in a dream.
She talks just like her mother.

blocks.text: *Gibi* takes the endings of **to be**: *Hasta gibisin* (You look ill), *Seni anlıyor gibiyim* (I think I understand you), *Yorgun gibiydi* (She seemed tired).
*Sanki* is one word, like *belki* and *çünkü*, although it contains the old *ki*. And *sanki* alone doesn't need *gibi*, but the two often go together: *Sanki beni duymuyormuş gibi*.

summary: `-mIş gibi` means **as if**: *olmamış gibi*, *anlamıyormuş gibi*, *ağlayacakmış gibi*; nouns and adjectives take `-(y)mIş`: *hastaymış gibi*. Never `-DI` before *gibi*.
A different subject adds its ending after `-mIş`: *suçluymuşum gibi baktı*.
`-mIş gibi yapmak` means **to pretend**: *Uyuyormuş gibi yaptı*; **pretend not to** negates the state: *duymamış gibi yaptı*. Colloquially, *numara yapmak*.
`-DIğI gibi` means **as**: *dediğim gibi*, *bildiğiniz gibi*, and in stories **as soon as**.
`-(y)AcAk gibi` is **it looks as if**: *Yağmur yağacak gibi*; `-(y)AcAk gibi olmak` is **to nearly**: *düşecek gibi oldum*.
*Sanki* opens a comparison, often with `-mIş gibi`; *tıpkı … gibi* is **just like**.
